newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Venezuela fishermen protest oil spill damage.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Venezuela fishermen protest oil spill damage.

text.p: About 300 fishing boats staged a protest in Venezuela's principal oil export artery Thursday to highlight the damage caused by an oil spill there in February.

The demonstration deepened a shipping crisis in Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela's oil heartland, which is costing the country $20 million per month in lost oil earnings and gaining the country a bad name in the international shipping community, industry sources say.
Eyewitnesses said the protest, led by local governor Francisco Arias Cardenas, passed off peacefully and oil tanker traffic in the Lake Maracaibo shipping channel was not affected.
The narrow stretch of water carries up to 1.5 million barrels per day of crude oil for export to the United States and Europe.
During the protest, Coast Guard vessels escorted oil tankers up to 660 feet (220 metres) long out of the channel, ensuring that none of the tiny fishing launches got in their way.

The fishermen, acting through environmental lawyer Tulio Alvarez, have demanded $292.5 million in damages from the owners of the Greek-flagged Nissos Amorgos oil tanker which spilled 25,000 barrels of crude after running aground on February 28.

But tanker owner representatives have called this an "insane number", pointing to international treaties which limit the liability of ship owners and provide for compensation only for proven lost earnings.

The Nissos Amorgos was one of four tankers to go aground seriously in the channel in the space of two months, prompting the transport minister to sack several directors of the state-run dredging authority INC.
But no one yet knows what caused the spill or the groundings.

In a report released Thursday, the congressional Environment Committee said strong winds and currents were probably to blame. They dismissed other theories including one suggesting a sunken wreck ripped open the Nissos hull and another that sloppy maintenance caused the channel to silt up.
However, a sonar survey of the channel floor was being conducted this week by the Venezuelan Navy and shippers say its findings could provide a definitive answer.

A draught restriction of 36 foot (12 meter) at high tide was imposed in the channel on April 18 as a precaution against further spills, but this has seriously disrupted Venezuela's exports. Shippers say the 3.5 foot (one meter) draught reduction means each tanker can carry less crude, increasing the per-barrel transport costs.
Also, insurance costs have surged since the spill.

One ship agent in Maracaibo said oil giants Exxon and Shell were both refusing to load oil in Lake Maracaibo until the problem was resolved, preferring instead to lift from a storage terminal in the Caribbean island of Bonaire.
He estimated that Venezuela was losing about 50 cents per barrel, or $20 million per month, because of the draught restriction and higher insurance costs.
The Nissos Amorgos and its captain have both been detained since the spill, which tanker owners say breaks all the international guidelines.
Intertanko, the international tanker owners association, took the unusual step of sending a representative to Venezuela this week to lobby for their release.

Insurance experts say two international treaties which apply in Venezuela, the Civil Liability Convention and the Fund Convention, provide for costs up to about $82 million, of which $7.2 million is paid by the tanker owner.

The Nissos Amorgos owners feel they have done enough by posting a $7.2 million guarantee in a Venezuelan bank and the insurers have opened two offices to receive claims for lost earnings caused by the spill.
Venezuela's Congress failed to approve a separate agreement called "Fund 92" which would have increased total spill cover to $200 million, the congressional report said.
((--Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2611))
